content: The prevalence of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and associated risks among women living with HIV (WLHIV) varies by age and immune status. Studies have shown that the prevalence of CIN 2+ is approximately 9% in WLHIV over the age of 30, 6% in those under 35-40 years, and 8% in those over 40 years. These findings highlight the importance of age-specific screening strategies for cervical precancerous lesions in WLHIV. For women with HIV who have a negative initial screening test for cervical precancerous lesions, the optimal rescreening interval remains a topic of investigation. Options include rescreening within 1, 2, or 3 years. Most studies included in the analysis used cytology as the baseline test, with some also incorporating HPV testing. The study periods ranged from 1994 to 2017, with earlier studies reflecting ART initiation at CD4 counts <200 cells/μL and later studies reflecting initiation at <350 cells/μL. The risk of bias in these studies was classified as moderate in six studies and low in two. Cumulative incidence data from several studies indicate that the risk of CIN 2+ in WLHIV varies by CD4 count. For example, at 5 years post-screening, the cumulative risk of CIN 2+ was 22% in WLHIV with CD4 counts <350 cells/μL, 12% in those with CD4 counts between 350-499 cells/μL, and 14% in those with CD4 counts >500 cells/μL. In comparison, the risk in HIV-negative women was 10%. These findings underscore the inverse relationship between CD4 count and cervical precancer risk. The recurrence of cervical lesions after treatment is higher in WLHIV compared to HIV-negative women. For instance, one study reported a 57% persistence or progression rate of CIN 2 at a maximum follow-up of 10 years. The recurrence rates were consistently higher in WLHIV across various studies, regardless of the treatment modality used (e.g., cryotherapy or LLETZ). This highlights the need for tailored follow-up strategies in this population. The impact of antiretroviral therapy (ART) on cervical cancer risk has evolved over time. Earlier studies, conducted before widespread access to effective ART, may not fully reflect the current risk landscape. ART has been shown to reduce the risk of precancer progression after immune reconstitution, but findings from earlier studies should be interpreted with caution. There is limited evidence to determine the appropriate age to initiate cervical cancer screening in WLHIV or the optimal frequency of screening. Histologically confirmed invasive cervical cancer (ICC) is rare before the age of 35-40, but CIN 2/3 lesions are observed in approximately 7% of screened WLHIV under 25 years and 11% under 30 years. Balancing early detection with screening frequency is critical, but data to guide these decisions are scarce. The literature also lacks studies on the risk of recurrence following a first negative test after treatment, as well as data on the cost-effectiveness and potential harms of screening at different ages and intervals. Additionally, there is a need for research on women’s preferences and values regarding screening and follow-up options. To address these gaps, an individual patient data meta-analysis (IPD-MA) is planned to provide age-specific evidence on cervical cancer screening initiation and frequency, including treatment follow-up. This effort aims to harmonize data and inform evidence-based recommendations for cervical cancer prevention in WLHIV.
